library(knitr)
library(secr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(MASS)

knitr::opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path="figures/01_spatial_caprecap-")

def.chunk.hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("chunk")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  chunk = function(x, options) {
    x <- def.chunk.hook(x, options)
    chunk_size <- if (is.null(options$size)) "normalsize" else options$size
    ifelse(
      chunk_size != "normalsize",
      paste0("\n \\", chunk_size, "\n\n", x, "\n\n \\normalsize"),
      x
    )
  }
)

hook_output <- knit_hooks$get("output")
knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  lines <- options$output.lines
  if (is.null(lines)) {
    return(hook_output(x, options))
  }
  x <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n"))
  more <- "..."
  if (length(lines) == 1) {
    if (length(x) > lines) {
      x <- c(head(x, lines), more)
    }
  } else {
    x <- c(more, x[lines], more)
  }
  x <- paste(c(x, ""), collapse = "\n")
  hook_output(x, options)
})

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this lecture and practical, you should be able to:

- Explain how spatial recaptures help estimate animal density and abundance.
- Understand and be able to compile encounter histories from survey data.
- Explain activity centres, distance-dependent detection and the state space.
- Recognise suitable survey methods and the need for reliable individual IDs.
- Explain key SCR assumptions and their consequences for survey design.
- Outline a field survey using the four-step planning and data workflow.
- Fit, compare, and interpret simple SCR models in R using `secr`.

## Spatial capture-recapture (SCR)

\small
\setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\small}
\setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate subbody}{size=\footnotesize}

- Uses \alert{spatially explicit} encounter histories 
    - fully described by a 3D $[n,J,K]$ array
    - *who* was detected (individual, $i=1,\dots,n$)
    - *when* (occasion, $k=1,\dots,K$)
    - & importantly \alert{\emph{where}} (trap, $j=1,\dots,J$)

\vspace{.25em}

- To construct a joint model of
    - a density model describing how animals are distributed in space
    - a detection model that describing probabilities of detecting those animals

\vspace{.25em}

- That allows one to test a range of ecological theories:  
    - density, abundance, demography
    - spatial variation in density
    - space use
    - landscape connectivity
    - movement/dispersal

## SCR data collection methods

\small
\setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\small}
\setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate subbody}{size=\footnotesize}

Many field methods for generating spatial capture-recapture data:

- live capture (direct)
    - \alert{physical marking}
    - eg, ear tags, bird bands, PIT tags...

\vspace{.5em}

- passive detection (direct)
    - \alert{ID by distinctive natural marks/calls}
    - eg, camera traps
    - eg, sound recorders

\vspace{.5em}

- non-invasive genetic sampling (indirect)
    - \alert{ID by genotype}
    - eg, scat from line transects
    - eg, hair from hair snares
    - eg, urine from scent posts

## Example: snow leopard -- camera traps

\vspace{0.35cm}
\roomyitems[0.9em]

**Natural marks identify the animal.**

\vspace{0.3cm}

- Place cameras across a mountain landscape; record station locations,
  operating dates and each encounter.
- Match flank patterns to identify the same cat at different stations.
- Analyse individual encounter histories with camera stations as
  **point detectors** (repeated images in a short time are one encounter).
- Place cameras so that recaptures at different cameras are likely.

<!-- Local context: ../slt_material/Fauna Species Bibliography and Conservation
Actors in Kyrgyzstan.docx, snow leopard section (including Sarychat-Ertash
camera monitoring). Field/method source: Sharma et al. (2020), PAWS Guidelines,
further_reading/PAWS-guidelines-2020.pdf, printed pp. 20--27, 33--36.
Illustrative survey, not a reported Kyrgyzstan estimate. This is the method
used in the practical. Do not treat photographs in a burst as independent
counts, or assume opposite flanks can always be matched. -->

## Example: otter -- DNA from spraints

\vspace{0.35cm}
\roomyitems[0.9em]

**Genetic identity replaces visible natural marks.**

\vspace{0.3cm}

- Extend local riverbank sign surveys by collecting fresh scat, with sample locations and GPS tracks of the searched routes.
- Laboratory analysis identifies species and individuals. The same otter's
  DNA at different locations provides spatial recaptures.
- Analyse detections together with **where was searched**.
- Consider movement along the river network when defining distances and
  habitat.

<!-- Local context: Davletbakov, A. T. / Ilbirs Foundation, Instructions for
monitoring the Central Asian otter, ../slt_material/methodology in English/
 Monitoring of otter_AD.docx: riverbank routes, spraints, tracks and cameras.
DNA collection and SCR are proposed extensions, not claims about that protocol.
Method example: Murphy, S. M., Adams, J. R., Waits, L. P. & Cox, J. J. (2021).
Evaluating otter reintroduction outcomes using genetic spatial capture--recapture
modified for dendritic networks. Ecology and Evolution 11: 15047--15061.
https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.8187
That study concerns North American river otters, NOT Kyrgyzstan's Lutra lutra;
the transferable lesson is network geometry, not a validated local model.
The appropriate model depends on whether local movement is river-confined.
Genotyping quality, sample age and repeat collection of the same deposit need
protocols. A network density denominator must be explicit (e.g. otters/100 km). -->

## Example: desert monitor -- marked animals

\vspace{0.35cm}
\roomyitems[0.9em]

**An individual mark can make repeat searches useful for SCR.**

\vspace{0.3cm}

- A trained, authorised team captures, uniquely marks and releases monitors at their capture locations.
- Revisit mapped search areas; record each marked animal's ID and exact
  location, together with search coverage and effort.
- Analyse these as **area-search detections**, rather than records from
  fixed camera stations.

<!-- Local context: Davletbakov, A. T. (2026), Guidelines for monitoring the
abundance and range of Desert monitor (Varanus griseus caspius) within the
Kyrgyz Republic, ../slt_material/methodology in English/Monitor Lizard_AD.docx:
visual routes, tracks/burrows, GPS, photographs and temperature/activity.
This is a hypothetical extension requiring species-specific marking and
feasibility assessment, not an existing local SCR protocol or a handling lesson.
Method source: Efford, M. (2011). Estimation of population density by spatially
explicit capture--recapture analysis of data from area searches.
Ecology 92: 2202--2207. https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0332.1
Its reptile example is the flat-tailed horned lizard, NOT Varanus griseus.
See also Efford, Polygon and transect detectors in secr:
https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-polygondetectors.pdf
Do not assume the species' stripes alone give validated individual photo-ID.
Record searched areas, including visits without detections; capture locations
alone do not define effort. Area search differs from single-catch trap sampling. -->

## Spatial capture-recapture (SCR): Detector types

\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}


: **SCR (`secr`) detector types**

| **Category** | **Type (conceptual)** | **`secr` name** |
|:----|:-----------------------------|:-------|
| **Point** | Single-capture trap (1 animal at a time) | single |
| | Multi-capture trap (multiple animals) | multi |
| | Proximity detector (non-exclusive detection) | proximity |
| | Count detector (multiple detections per occasion) | count |
| | Binary proximity with cap of 1 detection | capped |
| | Acoustic / signal-based detector | signal |
| **Area** | Area search detector | polygon |
| | Area search with independent subdetectors | polygonX |
| **Line** | Linear search detector | transect |
|  | Linear search with independent subdetectors | transectX |

## SCR: survey design

- Spatial recaptures tell us **how detection probabilities change with distance**. This is critical to estimating abundance.
- Arrays should cover **at least one home range**, preferably more, to
  sample enough individuals and their movements.
- Start with detector spacing of **1--2$\sigma$** to allow spatial recaptures;
  use pilot data to check the species' movement scale and detection rate.

```{r scr-survey-design, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=2.5, out.width="100%", out.height="1.45in"}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2.5, 0.3, 1.7, 0.3))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  layouts <- list(seq(-0.6, 0.6, length.out = 4),
                  seq(-6, 6, length.out = 4),
                  seq(-2.6, 2.6, length.out = 4))
  titles <- c("Too small", "Too spread out", "Just right")
  captions <- c("Limited coverage", "Few spatial recaptures",
                "Coverage + spatial recaptures")
  angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
  for (j in seq_along(layouts)) {
    xy <- expand.grid(x = layouts[[j]], y = layouts[[j]])
    plot(NA, xlim = c(-7, 7), ylim = c(-7, 7), asp = 1,
         axes = FALSE, ann = FALSE, xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
    rect(min(xy$x), min(xy$y), max(xy$x), max(xy$y),
         border = "grey60", lty = 2)
    lines(2.45 * cos(angle), 2.45 * sin(angle),
          col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
    points(xy$x, xy$y, pch = 19, col = "#008080", cex = 0.8)
    title(main = titles[j], cex.main = 1.05)
    mtext(captions[j], side = 1, line = 0.5, cex = 0.75)
  }
})
```

<!-- Source: Durbach, I., Micro-level survey design for secr, GSLEP/SLT:
https://globalsnowleopard.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/How-to-choose-where-to-setup-camera-traps-survey-design_-.pdf
Guidance: spacing 1--2 sigma and array coverage greater than one home range.
These are starting rules, not guarantees of sufficient animals or recaptures.
Original schematic: 16 detectors per panel; sigma = 1 in arbitrary units.
Circles have radius 2.45 sigma (approximately the 95% contour for isotropic
bivariate normal space use), not a hard limit on movement or detection.
The right-hand grid spacing is approximately 1.73 sigma, and its footprint
extends beyond the illustrated home range. The wide grid has 4 sigma spacing.
A large array is not inherently bad: the middle panel is too sparse for this
movement scale and fixed detector budget. All three are teaching diagrams,
not simulated captures or optimized survey designs. -->

## Spatial capture-recapture (SCR): Assumptions$^*$

| # | Assumption | Description |
|:--|:----------|:---------------------------|
| 1 | Population closure | No births, deaths, immigration, or emigration occur during the sampling period. |
| 2 | Fixed activity centres | Each individual has a stable activity centre that does not change during the study. |
| 3 | Distance-dependent detection | Detection probability declines monotonically with distance from an individual’s activity centre. |
| 4 | Independence of detections | Detection events are independent across individuals and sampling occasions (conditional on model parameters). |
| 5 | Correct individual identification | All individuals are uniquely and correctly identified with no mis-classification errors. |

## Spatial capture-recapture Terminology$^*$

\footnotesize

| Term | Definition |
|:-------|:----------------------------------------|
| Capture history | A record of detections for each individual across detectors and sampling occasions. |
| Detector (trap) | A device or method used to detect individuals (e.g., camera trap, hair snare, acoustic recorder). |
| Detector array | The spatial configuration of all detectors used in the study. |
| Effort | Information on when and where detectors were active; used to correctly model detection probability. |
| Activity centre | The latent (unobserved) central location of an individual’s home range, assumed fixed during the study. |
| State space | The spatial region that contains all possible activity centres of individuals in the population. |
| Mask | A discretized representation of the state space used in computation (grid of possible activity centre locations). |
| Buffer | An added margin around the detector array to ensure the state space includes all individuals that could be detected. |
